newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russian communist sees risk of chaos, dictatorship.
newsitem.headline: Russian communist sees risk of chaos, dictatorship.

text.p: Communist Party boss Gennady Zyuganov, urging ailing President Boris Yeltsin to resign for the sake of Russia, said on Thursday the nation was mired in crisis and risked chaos or dictatorship.

On a visit to France, Zyuganov predicted he would have a "good chance" of winning any new presidential election, saying Yeltsin had secured re-election in July with misleading promises and by hiding his heart problems.
Yeltsin beat Zyuganov by 54 to 40 percent in the July 3 run-off.

"If one thinks of the interests of Mr Yeltsin himself, of his family and of Russia, it would be much better for him to resign," Zyuganov told the French Institute for International Relations, reiterating appeals for Yeltsin to step down.

"There are forces which are pushing our country either towards chaos or towards dictatorship," he said after attending a session of the 39-nation Council of Europe in Strasbourg, eastern France, adding that either was unacceptable.
"There is great danger in Russia...there is a crisis of the non-payment of salaries, for teachers, for judges, for military officers. There is huge discontent," he said speaking through a translator.
Zyuganov said he would have a "good chance of winning another election...Electors understand that we didn't lie."
He accused Yeltsin of misleading voters about the state of his health and of breaking a promise that a backlog of salaries would be paid.
Doctors said on Wednesday that Yeltsin was fit enough to have heart surgery but they delayed his planned bypass operation for at least six weeks to improve the chances of success.
Zyuganov said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, security supremo Alexander Lebed and Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov were jostling for power in the vacuum left by the ailing Yeltsin.

In Moscow, Lebed painted a similar picture of instability, sounding a warning that Russia was on the brink of chaos and the army could mutiny. "We are at a dangerous limit, a very dangerous limit," he told a news conference.

Zyuganov said Lebed was "a good general but the army and the art of politics are not the same thing". He said Lebed entered the Yeltsin camp only when he knew that the president was sick and would be incapacitated in office.
He also said Lebed's peace pact with rebels in the breakaway Russian region of Chechnya did not go far enough, and said that the region should not be granted full independence.

Zyuganov also said that he opposed expansion of NATO and that the world had been less unpredictable in the days of the Cold War when Moscow and Washington, for instance, could together resolve the 1962 Cuban missile crisis.
"The situation today is much more dangerous because in a uni-polar world, the United States can take decisions almost alone to bombard foreign capitals," he said.
He said he opposed enlargement of NATO and said Communists might not ratify treaties limiting nuclear weapons. "If NATO is enlarged, arms accords will be threatened," he said.
